body:
Markets at record highs. Confidence at a 70-year low.

Most of that fear is one quiet question: "Will AI take my job?"

The honest version:

AI won't replace most people.
People who know how to use AI will.

That divide doesn't care about your title, your degree, or how "technical" you are. It only cares whether you've learned to direct these tools.

I watch people with zero coding background pick up Claude and, in weeks, do work that used to take a team.

The tools aren't the hard part anymore. Knowing what's possible is.

We're still incredibly early. ⚡

Which side of that gap do you want to be on?
notes: Short-punchy variant. Won the informal head-to-head vs post-002. Impressions grew 164 → 202 over 7 days (+23%).

topic: AI replacing jobs / market-vs-confidence divergence (long version)
body:
Last week the headlines said it all:

Stock market at record highs.
Consumer confidence at a 70-year low.

A lot of that fear comes down to one question people are scared to say out loud:

"Is AI going to take my job?" 😬

Here's the honest answer most people won't give you.

AI isn't going to replace most workers.

People who know how to use AI will.

That's the real divide forming right now — and it has nothing to do with your job title, your degree, or how "technical" you think you are.

I keep watching people with zero coding background pick up Claude and within weeks:

🧠 do the work of an entire research team
⚡ automate tasks that used to eat their whole week
📊 build tools they were told they'd have to hire for
🚀 finally move on ideas they'd sat on for years

The tools aren't the hard part anymore.

The bottleneck is knowing what's possible — and how to direct it.

That's the whole reason I teach this.

Not because AI is magic.
Because the gap between people who use it well and people who don't is about to become the biggest career advantage of the decade.

We are still incredibly early. ⚡

The Wall Street vs. Main Street gap is real.
But on the individual level, which side you land on is far more in your control than the headlines make it feel.

If you learned to use AI properly this year, what's the first thing you'd take off your plate? 👀
notes: Long-form variant. Grew 79 → 120 over 7 days (+52%). Short still wins head-to-head but the ratio narrowed from 2.08x to 1.68x — long-form has slower-burn growth.

topic: non-technical people are winning AI hackathons
body:
Hackathon winners used to be engineers in hoodies.

Now they're lawyers. Doctors. Operations managers.
People who couldn't write a line of code six months ago.

They just learned what to ask for.

That's the part most people still don't see — the barrier to building isn't technical anymore. It's knowing what's possible and how to direct it.

I watch this happen at Network School every week. People with zero coding background ship working tools in a weekend.

If you've been telling yourself "I'm not a tech person, so this isn't for me" — that excuse is expired. ⚡

What would you build first if you actually believed you could?
notes: Posted text-only. Hashtags trimmed to 3 (vs post-001's 4). Underperformed post-001 at same age — possibly the topic (hackathons) was too niche, or 3-hashtag trim hurt discoverability vs 4.

topic: $10k-$37,500 hidden cost of doing email yourself (corrected math version)
body:
"I'll just clear my email" is a five-figure decision.

If you spend the first hour of every workday on email, that's 250 hours a year.

Multiply that by what your time actually bills at. For a $40/hr freelancer, that's $10,000. For a $150/hr consultant, $37,500. Either way, a real number.

Nobody hires their best version of themselves to do inbox triage. But that's exactly who's doing it in most small businesses.

I keep meeting owners who've automated nothing in their first hour and everything in their last hour. That's backwards.

What's the first hour of your day actually worth, if you weren't doing email?
notes: Weakest June post so far at 77 imp / 4 days. Hypothesis: the multi-rate middle section ($40, $150) forced reader to do math and may have lost momentum. Compare to post-005 which has one clean number (4 hrs → 200 hrs) and 3.4× the reach.

topic: 4 hours/week of copy-pasting = 1 month vacation skipped
body:
4 hours a week.

That's what most small-business owners spend pasting things between tools. Email to spreadsheet. Form responses to CRM. Notion to Slack.

Over a year, that's 200 hours.

That's a one-month vacation you're not taking, because you're moving information from one box to another like it's 1998.

The frustrating part: it's the easiest kind of work to hand off. Not strategic. Not relationship-driven. Just copy, paste, format, send, on repeat.

Where did the 4 hours come from for you this week?
notes: Best Jun performer (261 imp / 3 days). One concrete number (4 hrs) + a visceral comparison (1 month vacation) + a date-stamp (1998) for memorability. Replies sent to both commenters in Alex voice (warm, no pitch, reacts to specific phrase).

topic: most expensive workflow is the one only you can do
body:
The most expensive workflow in your business isn't the one that costs you money.

It's the one only you can do.

Every hour you spend on it is an hour you can't spend on the work nobody else can replace — selling, closing, building, deciding.

For a $250/hr consultant, an hour of admin you do yourself is a $250 spend. You just don't see the invoice.

That's why a $200 setup that hands one of those workflows off pays for itself before lunch.

What's the one task only you can do — that you'd hand off tomorrow if you could?
notes: Stage-1 funnel violation: contained '$200 setup pays for itself before lunch' pitch line. Underperformed at half post-005's reach in same 24h. Confirms hypothesis: stage-mismatched pitching hurts Problem-Unaware posts. Comments stayed generic, no real-customer-ICP engagement. Post version was corrected AFTER it went live (post-03.txt now has the clean version for next run).

topic: permission to stop doing low-value work, not productivity
body:
You don't have a productivity problem.

You have a permission-to-stop-doing-the-low-value-work problem.

Most owners I've talked to could automate a third of their week tomorrow. They don't, because somewhere along the line they decided that doing the work themselves was part of being a serious operator.

It isn't. It's part of being a busy one.

The people who break out of that aren't more disciplined. They've just given themselves permission to stop.

What's the one thing you'd stop doing this week if nobody could question it?
notes: Strongest engagement of June (5 substantive comments + 6 reactions in 24h). Reframing 'productivity = permission problem' got real engagement — Maleeha's reply is the standout (long, substantive, agrees + extends with own experience). Stage 2 (Problem Aware) posted out-of-schedule order (was supposed to be Jun-10). Worth understanding why this one hit vs post-006 dud — likely: zero pitch + reframing nail.

topic: client update email, 3 hours to 4 minutes, same tone
body:
Small business owners I work with used to spend 3 hours every Monday writing the same client update email.

Now it takes 4 minutes.

Same information. Same tone. Just not their Sunday night anymore.

What's the task that eats the start of your week?
